description:
Blazing-fast Claude in your terminal — a C++26 alternative to claude-code.

agentty is a native C++26 terminal coding agent and a drop-in alternative to claude-code. A single static binary with sub-millisecond cold start, sandboxed by default, and one-command SSH air-gap. No Node, Python, or Electron. Signs in with your Claude Pro/Max subscription or an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
Fixed
- An oversized SKILL.md no longer costs a real skill its place. Files too
  large to load are kept so agentty skills can name them, but they used to
  count against AGENTTY_MAX_SKILLS — three of them at the cap silently
  pushed three working skills out of the catalog. Only loadable skills count
  now.
- A buffering gateway no longer hides the status bar. When a proxy holds
  the model's output back, the whole status row used to turn into "network
  gateway is buffering output — waiting…", re-armed every 15 s, so the
  context gauge and everything else vanished for the length of the stream.
  The phase chip now just reads buffered… until the burst lands.
- The Skills panel stays inside the terminal. Its header and its detail
  footer are rows the list does not get, and the shared viewport estimate only
  knew the two-row hint chrome — so on a short terminal the panel grew taller
  than the screen and painted the list straight over its own footer, which is
  where the description, the findings and the caveat live. The list budget is
  now derived from what the panel actually spends, blank spacer rows yield
  first when it is still too tight, and a footer line that wraps keeps its
  indent instead of snapping back to column 0.
Added
- The prompt cache sits next to the context gauge. CACHE 94% on the
  status bar: how much of the prefix the last request left warm was served
  from cache. A healthy hit is just the number, in green. Anything else says
  why in one word, so a 0% never leaves you guessing: 0% new for an
  expected cold start (new thread, compaction, a model switch), 3% idle
  when a long pause simply outlived the cache, and 2% miss in amber when a
  prefix that should have been warm was re-priced from scratch — the one
  that costs you 10-20x on time-to-first-token. Hosts that never report
  cache use read n/a. Judged against what the previous request left warm,
  so a big new tool output does not look like a miss. On narrow terminals
  the word goes first, then the number, before the phase or the context
  gauge. The context bar itself now shows the same split: the part of the
  window served from cache draws as ▓, the part paid in full this
  request as █ — same width, readable without colour.
- The plan is always in view. The composer footer's empty middle now
  carries the agent's plan: a task meter, 3/7 and the item in flight
  (●), or the next one up (○) between steps — no ^T needed. It is
  responsive at every width: the label shortens with …, then drops to the
  meter and the count, and steps aside entirely before it would ever push
  the model badge or the mode chip off the row. An unfinished plan stays
  when the agent stops ("stopped at 3/7"); a finished one shows its ✓
  for the rest of the turn and then goes quiet. Switching threads swaps in
  that thread's plan instead of leaving the last one up.
- The skill catalog says what it is leaving out. agentty skills and the
  Skills panel (Ctrl+K) now report N of M cataloged · cap C · K not cataloged instead of listing a truncated catalog as if it were the whole
  library — the failure mode where a skill you installed is simply absent.
  The installed count rides along with the cached discovery, so it costs no
  extra walk, and the panel stays silent when everything fits. Every other
  reason a skill is missing gets its own line and its own fix — too large to
  load, unreadable or nameless, hidden by a same-named skill — and the cap
  knob is only suggested when the cap is the reason (#134, thanks
  @davidwed).
- The Plugins pane shows the tool cap and what it refused. The header now
  names the per-request maximum (the provider's limit, your
  AGENTTY_MCP_TOOL_BUDGET, or "no cap" on providers that defer schemas),
  how many tools are deferred and addressable by name, and how many were left
  out — split into "by the cap" (pin it with p) and "by an invalid schema"
  (only the server can fix it). Previously a tool the cap refused looked
  exactly like one the model searches for.
